Ten Claude Styles
MADE WITH CLAUDE · LAB EDU · 00:00:42:22

Ten worlds.Zero design tools.

A 42-second edu reel where Claude animates ten completely different art styles, from a blueprint heist to a neon light cycle. One master prompt: Claude Code wrote the script, timed an ElevenLabs voice word by word, and drew every world in code on an HTML canvas, with four builders working in parallel. This is the full workflow, and all ten prompts.

01 · The idea

One card, ten worlds.

The claim is simple: Claude can animate completely different visual worlds, and none of them comes from a design tool. The proof is showing ten of them back to back, fast enough to feel like a flex and slow enough to read each one.

So the reel is a machine with one stage: a big card in the middle. Every style is typed as a prompt into a command bar above it, the world renders in, the whole background floods to that world's colour and props jump out of the card on the stressed words. A list of ten pills fills as it goes, number 10 stays hidden as "???" until the finale, and the outro shrinks everything into a clean grid of all ten.

02 · References

What Claude needed before the first prompt.

This is the Lab's own piece. These are the ideas it leans on, described in general terms.

The "one tool, many styles" showcase

A common format on social: one frame that cycles through looks with a numbered list. The plain version is a static card on a light background, which is where we started and what we had to push past (see Watch out).

Ten generic art styles

Blueprint, Japanese woodblock, woodcut, pop-up book, 1930s rubber hose cartoon, transit map, stained glass, risograph, exploded-view teardown and neon light cycle. All are traditions or techniques, not anyone's brand; every world is drawn from scratch, and the light cycle is an original bike.

A prompt you can see

A chat-style command bar above the card types each style as a slash command and presses send. The viewer watches the input become the output, which is the whole point of the reel.

Word-cued kinetic motion

Every stressed word changes something: a stamp slams, a seal lands, a train leaves the card. Between words, the world inside the card keeps moving, so there is no frozen frame.

Palette

The Lab's colours carry the frame and the outro. Each world brings its own background colour, alternating light and dark.

#F6F0E6 cream#D97757 clay#141A2E navy
Presenter

Catalina, the Lab's character, from her real images: two short image-to-video clips for the opening and the close, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, in her own corner.

03 · One-time setup

Before the prompt.

Step 01

Install Claude Code.

Follow the official guide at docs.claude.com (Claude Code overview) for your system, then open it inside an empty project folder.

Step 02

Node 22+ and FFmpeg.

The scenes are plain JavaScript drawing on an HTML canvas. Node runs a headless browser that renders each frame, and FFmpeg turns the frames and the audio into the final MP4.

Step 03

Python 3.10+.

For the audio side: checking loudness, mixing the voice with the sound effects and reading the narration back with Whisper to confirm every word.

Step 04

An ElevenLabs API key.

Put it in a .env file in the project and ask Claude to request word-level timestamps with the audio. Those timestamps are what every cut and every cue reads.

Optional

A style guide for Claude.

A short Markdown file with your palette, fonts, pacing and safe zone, which Claude reads before writing any scene. We used a paid motion-design guide; your own notes work too.

04 · Claude session

One prompt, then the checks.

Everything started from one master prompt, followed by two quality-control messages: the stills review and the final render.

00:01 · master prompt · claude code
Make a 42-second vertical edu reel for The AI Editing Lab, 1080x1920 at 30 fps, all in English. Topic: Claude can animate ten completely different visual worlds without a single design tool.

1. Script. Hook in under 2 seconds: "Claude can animate ten completely different worlds, without a single design tool." Then a tease ("Here are all ten, and the last one is everyone's favorite."), then the ten styles, one line each: the style name, then its world in five words or fewer (Blueprint, a heist on a floor plan · Ukiyo-e, a wave from old Japan · Woodcut, a ninja in black ink · Pop-up book, a picnic that unfolds · Rubber hose, cartoons from the thirties · Transit map, every line on time · Stained glass, light through color · Risograph, a poster in two inks · Teardown, a machine pulled apart · And light cycle, neon on a grid). Close with: "All plain code. Comment STYLES and I'll send you all ten prompts."

2. Voice. Generate the narration with ElevenLabs, voice "Jessica", at natural speed (1.0). Save the start and end time of every word to words.json. Every cut and every animation cue reads its time from a word: each style starts on its spoken name.

3. The frame. One big 16:9 card in the middle of the screen where each style plays for about 3 seconds. Above it, a command bar that types the style as a prompt ("/style blueprint — a heist on a floor plan"), presses send, and the new world scans in over the old one. Under it, the label "01 · Blueprint". A numbered 1-10 list of chunky pills fills as we go, with number 10 hidden as "???" until the end. On every style the full background floods to a colour that belongs to that world, alternating light and dark so each change is felt.

4. The worlds. Each style is a pure function of time drawn inside the card, on a 960x540 design box, with something moving from frame 0 and one hero moment around 1.5 seconds. The same function must also read as a small thumbnail at its final state. Every world is original: generic art styles, no copied characters, logos or film references.

5. Break the card. On the stressed words of each line, props jump out of the card onto the frame: a stamp, a seal, ink splats, a train, light rays, flying parts. Each set fades in its last 0.2 seconds.

6. Outro. Dark navy #141A2E floods out from the card, the last card shrinks into a clean 2x5 grid of all ten worlds, a small code window types STYLES[10], and "Comment STYLES" slams in clay.

7. Layout and look. Lab colours for the frame: cream #F6F0E6, clay #D97757, navy #141A2E; a bold grotesque with italic serif accent words, small mono labels at the top. Keep every text and prop inside x 90-960 and y 250-1480, and keep the bottom-left corner (x 0-520, y 1220 down) empty: our presenter goes there later.

8. Build. Agree one contract first (STYLES[n] = { name, tag, draw(K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) }), then build in parallel: one builder for the frame, hook and outro, three for the ten worlds. Sparse sound effects on real events, the voice always on top, mixed to -14 LUFS with a true peak at or below -1.5 dB.

9. Process. Show me a stills sheet before the final render and wait for my approval.

What came back: the script, the ElevenLabs narration with 95 time-stamped words, a shared contract for the ten worlds, and four scene builders running in parallel: one for the frame, the hook and the outro, three for the ten worlds (four, three and three). Each world is a pure function of time, so the frame can play it big in the card or small in the outro grid.

00:02 · stills before render · claude code
Before the final render, export a stills sheet: one frame every 1.5 seconds starting at frame 0, with a red outline for the safe zone (x 90-960, y 250-1480). Check every style for three things. Motion: does something visibly change at least once a second and on every stressed word, or is there a frozen stretch? Originality: is every world drawn for this script, with no generic placeholder and nothing that copies an existing film, character or logo? Readability: can every label, pill and prop be read on a phone, with enough contrast against that style's background? List every flat moment and every small or low-contrast element, fix them all in one pass and show me the sheet again.

What came back: the first pass looked flat: one static card on cream for 30 seconds, with a list too small to read on a phone. The fix was one pass with a command bar that types each style, a background flood per world, props that break out of the card on the stressed words, chunky pills for the list and a clean 2×5 grid for the outro.

00:03 · final render · claude code
Approved. Now composite our presenter Catalina on top from her real images: her two short image-to-video clips at the start and at the end, and full-body poses from her character sheet in between, in the bottom-left corner. Each pose swaps in place with a short crossfade on a beat change; she never slides in or out. Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps, encode H.264 at 14 Mbps CBR with the mix at -14 LUFS, and give me a stills strip of the final.

What came back: 42.7 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, H.264 at 14 Mbps, the voice mixed to −14 LUFS.

05 · What Claude built

Ten worlds on one contract.

THE CONTRACT

A world is a function

Every style is draw(K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur): it gets a canvas, a box and the seconds since it started, and nothing else. No state, so any frame can be rendered alone, at any size.

THE BAR

Typed, sent, rendered

A command bar types "/style name — its line" just before the name is spoken, presses send, and the new world scans in top to bottom over the old one in a third of a second.

THE FLOOD

A colour per world

On each spoken name the full background floods from the card centre to that world's colour, alternating light and dark, and the text ink flips with it.

THE PROPS

Out of the card

A separate props file draws over the whole frame: stamps, seals, ink splats, a punched ticket, light rays, flying parts. Each one is tied to a word of that line.

key code · styles_1to4.js + styles_8to10.js · the shared contract
// Contract: STYLES[n] = { name, tag, draw(K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) }.
// The caller has already done K.save(); K.translate(x, y); clipped to w×h,
// so every draw() paints in LOCAL coords 0..w × 0..h. Each world is designed
// on a 960×540 base and scaled by (w/960, h/540), so it also reads as a
// 280×158 thumbnail (the outro grid calls it with lt = dur).
// Pure functions of lt: no state, randomness only from seeded rngs.
function world(K, w, h, fn) { K.save(); K.scale(w / 960, h / 540); fn(); K.restore(); }

STYLES[1] = {
  name: 'Blueprint', tag: 'a heist on a floor plan',
  draw(K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) { world(K, w, h, () => blueprint(K, lt, dur)); },
};
STYLES[8]  = { name: 'Risograph',   tag: 'two inks · halftone · misregistration', draw: (K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) => drawRiso(K, w, h, lt, dur) };
STYLES[9]  = { name: 'Teardown',    tag: 'exploded view · callouts',              draw: (K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) => drawTeardown(K, w, h, lt, dur) };
STYLES[10] = { name: 'Light cycle', tag: 'neon · grid · speed',                   draw: (K, x, y, w, h, lt, dur) => drawLightCycle(K, w, h, lt, dur) };
key code · common_frame.js · the command bar
// the command bar: every style is typed as a prompt, SEND pulses, the card renders in
const frPrompt = n => '/style ' + FR_NAMES[n - 1].toLowerCase() + ' — ' + FR_PROMPT_TXT[n - 1];
const frTypeT  = n => FR_S[n - 1] - FR_BAR.lead;                             // typing starts just before the name is spoken
const frSendT  = n => frTypeT(n) + frPrompt(n).length / FR_BAR.cps + 0.03;  // ≈ name + 0.25 s
const FR_RENDER = 0.34;                                                      // scan-in of the new world after SEND
key code · common_frame.js · one background per world
// every style owns a full-frame colour that matches its world, alternating light/dark.
// Each change is a circle flood from the card centre. dark → light ink; acc = accent that reads on it.
const FR_BG = {
  1:  { c: '#16325C', dark: 1, acc: '#F08A64' },   // Blueprint
  2:  { c: '#F3E6CF', dark: 0, acc: '#C4552F' },   // Ukiyo-e
  3:  { c: '#111111', dark: 1, acc: '#F05A3E' },   // Woodcut
  4:  { c: '#CFE3B4', dark: 0, acc: '#A8431F' },   // Pop-up book
  5:  { c: '#E9C98B', dark: 0, acc: '#8E3418' },   // Rubber hose
  6:  { c: '#EAF2F7', dark: 0, acc: '#C4552F' },   // Transit map
  7:  { c: '#2A1640', dark: 1, acc: '#F2A27F' },   // Stained glass
  8:  { c: '#FF8FB1', dark: 0, acc: '#141A2E' },   // Risograph
  9:  { c: '#F2C14E', dark: 0, acc: '#7A2A10' },   // Teardown
  10: { c: '#0B0F2A', dark: 1, acc: '#F08A64' },   // Light cycle
  navy: { c: '#141A2E', dark: 1, acc: '#F08A64' }, // outro
};
// the background timeline: one flood per style on its spoken name, navy at the outro
const FR_BGSEG = [[0, 'paper', 0]]
  .concat(FR_S.slice(0, 10).map((s, i) => [s, i + 1, 0.34]))
  .concat([[CUT_OUT, 'navy', 0.36]]);
key code · fr_props.js · props on the words
// 02 · Ukiyo-e — "a wave from old Japan." Every prop is cued on a spoken word.
const tWave = wi(32), tOld = wi(34), tJapan = wi(35);   // wi(n) = start of word n

// three woodblock birds fly out of the card's top edge on "old"
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  const dt = t - tOld - i * 0.1; if (dt < 0) continue;
  const u = E.outCubic(clamp(dt / 1.2));
  const x = lerp(700 + i * 40, 860 + i * 66, u),
        y = lerp(660 + i * 30, 478 + i * 26, u) + Math.sin(dt * 5 + i) * 8;
  const fl = Math.sin(dt * 14 + i * 2);                  // wing flap
  K.save(); K.translate(x, y); K.scale(1.3, 1.3);
  K.beginPath(); K.moveTo(-30, -fl * 14);
  K.quadraticCurveTo(-14, -4, 0, 4); K.quadraticCurveTo(14, -4, 30, -fl * 14);
  K.lineWidth = 6; K.strokeStyle = '#1D2A44'; K.lineCap = 'round'; K.stroke();
  K.restore();
}
// the red hanko seal slams over the card's bottom-right corner on "Japan"
const sl = fpSlam(t, tJapan, 2.2);                      // big → 1 with a ring
if (sl.a > 0) {
  K.save(); K.globalAlpha *= sl.a; K.translate(950, 975); K.rotate(7 * D2R); K.scale(sl.s, sl.s);
  rr(K, -86, -86, 172, 172, 18); K.fillStyle = '#C8281E'; K.fill();
  // ...original, abstract carved marks in paper colour
  K.restore();
}
LEVEL UP

Four builders at once

Once the contract was fixed, four Claude agents built in parallel: one wrote the frame, the hook, the props and the outro, and three wrote the ten worlds. Because every world draws in its own box and only reads time, the pieces snapped together without seams, and a world that wasn't finished yet simply showed a neutral card instead of breaking the preview.

All ten, ready to paste.

Style 01 · background #16325C

Blueprint · a heist on a floor plan

prompt 01 · blueprint
/style blueprint — a heist on a floor plan

Blueprint style: a technical floor plan on deep blueprint blue (#16325C) with a fine white grid, thin white walls and doors, small mono room labels (VAULT, SECURITY, LOBBY, ARCHIVE, ENTRY) and a title block with a mission name and a running clock. A dotted red heist route sneaks room to room from the entry to the vault, and the vault dial spins and cracks open. Around the card: a flashlight beam sweeps, a TOP SECRET stamp slams on "heist", red push-pins pin the corners on "floor" and "plan". Draw it in code on an HTML canvas inside a 960x540 card, as a pure function of time (no state, seeded randomness only), with something moving from frame 0 and the hero moment at about 1.5 seconds. At its final state it must still read as a small thumbnail. Original drawing only: no copied characters, logos or film references.

08 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Show the input

The command bar makes the claim visible: each world starts as a line of text and becomes a picture in a third of a second.

02

Each style starts on its name

Every cut sits on the spoken name of the style, so what you hear and what you see change in the same frame.

03

Light, dark, light

Background colours alternate light and dark, so ten changes in 30 seconds still feel like ten distinct worlds.

04

Save the best for last

The tease promises a favourite, the list hides number 10 as "???", and the light cycle closes the run.

05

Thumbnails for free

Because every world is a function of time, the outro grid just calls the same ten functions at a small size and their final moment.

06

A corner for the presenter

The bottom-left is kept empty in every scene, so Catalina never covers a world and no prop ever lands on her.

09 · Watch out

What went wrong, and the fix.

The plain format looks flat

Copying the usual showcase, one static card on a cream background, looked flat: ten styles, and the frame never changed. The fix: a background colour per style with real contrast, a command bar that types each style, and props that break out of the card on the stressed words.

A small list is unreadable on a phone

The numbered list of styles started as small text and disappeared on a phone screen. The fix: chunky pills, with the current style in clay and the finished ones in ink.

A messy outro grid

The first closing grid of ten thumbnails looked scattered and uneven. The fix: a clean 2×5 grid, every tile the same size, kept to one side so the presenter's corner stays free.

Read the voice back

Run the narration through Whisper before animating. Every cut starts on a style's spoken name, so a misheard or drifting word moves a whole style off its cue.

10 · Ship it

From render to post.

The render is not the finish line. These steps decide how the reel looks once Instagram compresses it.

Step 01

Export at a real bitrate.

Halftone dots, thin blueprint lines and neon glow smear when compressed. Encode at 14 Mbps CBR.

Step 02

Check the loudness.

Aim for −14 LUFS with a true peak at or below −1.5 dB, and keep the voice above the sound effects.

Step 03

Make the cover.

The profile grid crops covers to 3:4, so keep the title and the main image between y 240 and 1680 (safer: 300 to 1480).

Step 04

Caption with the credits.

Say what was made and how, give the comment keyword, and credit the voice. On ElevenLabs' free plan, credit it as "Voice: ElevenLabs".
